A new survey by the progressive polling organization Data for Progress, shared exclusively with the Guardian, found that 61% of American likely voters believe extreme weather events have become more frequent over the past five years. The Guardian published the findings on July 19, framing them against ongoing political efforts in the United States to dismiss or downplay the connection between the climate crisis and severe weather. ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study))

Support for that view extends well beyond one party's base. According to the Guardian, 72% of Democratic respondents agreed that extreme weather events have increased, as did 63% of Independents and nearly half of Republicans — 46%. That last figure is notable given the Trump administration's repeated characterization of climate change as a hoax and broader political efforts, the Guardian reports, to suppress public discussion of the crisis.

The poll also probed what voters believe about specific weather types, asking whether each has been made worse by climate change. Heatwaves drew the widest acknowledgment: the Guardian reports that 67% of all respondents said climate change is intensifying them. Among Republican respondents specifically, 48% agreed on heatwaves — which the Guardian identifies as the highest share that Republicans reached for any individual weather category the survey tested.

Agreement extended across other weather types as well. The Guardian reports that 64% of respondents linked wildfires to climate worsening; 63% said the same for droughts; 62% for flooding and flash flooding; and 59% each for hurricanes and for severe thunderstorms with hailstorms. ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study))

Anthony Leiserowitz, who leads the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told the Guardian that the Data for Progress results are consistent with conclusions Yale's own surveys have reached. The Guardian reports he pointed to a pattern across polling of Americans increasingly drawing a connection between extreme weather events and heatwaves on one hand and the climate crisis on the other — and also expressing support for policies that would protect workers facing extreme heat.

Jennifer Marlon, a senior research scientist at Yale who focuses on climate communications, told the Guardian that despite the apparent consensus visible in the Data for Progress findings, many Americans still do not clearly understand that the climate is changing due to human activity. A spring survey from the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, the Guardian reports, found that 27% of respondents believed recent climate changes are mostly the result of natural processes. Marlon indicated that a widespread assumption — that global warming is probably part of a natural cycle — remains one of the most significant misconceptions the research continues to encounter. ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study))

Grace Adcox, a senior strategist at Data for Progress, told the Guardian that the poll findings point toward a bipartisan opening in conversations about extreme weather and climate. She observed that nearly everyone in the United States has encountered unusually hot conditions in recent years, and that regional differences in extreme weather exposure shape how voters perceive these events. Adcox also said that political attempts to polarize or suppress concern about climate change may not constitute a reliable success, the Guardian reports.

Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat, told the Guardian that politicians have for too long engaged in what he terms "climate-hushing" — quietly stepping back from public acknowledgment of the severe consequences of global warming. The Guardian reports he described the new polling data as evidence that elected officials should be engaging with climate openly rather than going silent on the issue.

High temperatures, floods, hurricanes, and tornadoes claim lives across the United States every year, the Guardian notes, providing the material stakes against which these shifts in public perception play out. ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jul/19/climate-crisis-us-voters-study))
